## In brief - Army chief Roos: Switzerland is target for Russia - Hybrid threats on European critical infrastructure - 80% of unauthorized drones from tourists, 20% unknown - Lack of anti-missile system, Patriot delayed
## Key facts - **What**: Statement from army chief on Russian threats to Switzerland - When: Recent interview on SRF (January 2026 at the head of the army) - Where: Zurich, Switzerland - Who: Benedikt Roos, 61 years old, corps commander and army chief - Reasons: Critical infrastructure (electricity, gas, north-south corridors, data centers) - Gaps: Lack of anti-missile defense and insufficient anti-drone capabilities - Main concern: Poor awareness among Swiss population
Switzerland is in Russia's crosshairs. This is what Benedikt Roos, 61, head of the Swiss armed forces since last January, said in an interview with SRF that leaves no room for interpretation. 'Yes,' he replied when asked the direct question: 'Is Switzerland a target for Moscow?'.
### Why Switzerland is a target
According to the commander, the reason lies in the country's geopolitical position and the infrastructure it possesses. 'Switzerland has critical infrastructure that is important for all of Europe: the distribution of electricity and gas, the main north-south links, major data centers'. These services are fundamental to the functioning of the economy and to the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) of all residents. An actor like Russia could strike precisely these points to destabilize all of Europe.
Roos frames the risk in a perspective of systemic confrontation. 'It is a struggle between systems: the liberal and democratic world against the autocratic one. More than ever we are part of the Western world and are therefore a potential target'. Not only direct military attacks, then, but hybrid threats capable of compromising essential services.
### The concrete danger of drones
In Leipzig, German authorities found drones full of explosives. In Switzerland, Roos's data are alarming. 'We are detecting more activity in this sector. We have more drone flights over critical infrastructure. Fortunately without bombs, but it could happen to us as well'.
On unauthorized overflights of drones over Swiss military facilities, the army chief is explicit: 80% come from tourists and private individuals. The remaining 20%, however, remains unknown. 'For the 20% we are not certain and cannot attribute them with clarity. We are pursuing some cases criminally in collaboration with the police and we still do not know who is behind them'.
The greater deficit remains poor awareness among the population. 'This is the decisive point. Awareness is not there yet. Fortunately for us, we no longer have memory of what war means. The awareness that Switzerland could enter a crisis is not yet deeply rooted,' Roos concludes. ### Missile Defense Gaps
The head of the army does not hide a fact that should worry all Swiss residents: Switzerland does not have a reliable missile defense system. Asked directly about the previous statement that Switzerland "would have nothing in terms of missile defense", Roos does not deny. "Yes, that's right, when we talk about defense against cruise or ballistic missiles. We have big gaps here. "
The Patriot system, which is supposed to fill this gap, is lagging behind and costs are rising. "The new Patriot system suffers delays and becomes more expensive: we are therefore evaluating alternatives to fill this gap more quickly." It means that Switzerland, at the moment, does not have adequate protection against threats that could come from the sky.
### Boosting anti-drone capabilities
Roos' concern is also about speed in bridging the gap. The armed forces have made progress, but insufficient. “We're upgrading our capabilities. The number of small reconnaissance drones supplied to troops has increased tenfold in a year. Now we need to make progress in defense against drones. This is one of the gaps that we urgently need to fill. "
Decreasing reconnaissance by drone is useful, but if you can't shoot down enemy drones it remains a vulnerability. The army knows to hurry.

item.description: CoG investigation: no fixed price in the contract. Viola Amherd informed the government 7-8 months late. Serious gaps in federal transparency.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - The Management Commission of the National Council heavily criticizes the F-35A negotiations - No fixed price contractually agreed with the USA according to the MC - Viola Amherd informed the Federal Council with a 7-8 month delay (August 2024 → March 2025) - External law firm excludes armasuisse's internal legal service from the negotiations
## Key Facts - **Who**: Management Commission (MC) of the National Council - What: Investigation into F-35A negotiations and breach of information transparency - When: August 2024 (first signs of additional costs) → March 2025 (information to the Federal Council) - Where: Bern; negotiations conducted with the United States - Key figure: Viola Amherd, former defense minister (DDPS) - Outcome: MC judges the organization of negotiations and delayed communication as 'inadequate'
### The MC report: no fixed price agreed
The Management Commission of the National Council investigated the negotiations for the purchase of F-35A jets, concluding that 'no fixed lump-sum price was agreed with the USA'. The MC's judgment is severe: the Federal Department of Defense, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS) and the then defense minister Viola Amherd conducted the negotiations in an 'inadequate' manner.
The most serious problem concerns the gap between what was stated publicly and the contractual facts. The DDPS communicated to Parliament and the public with 'absolute certainty' the existence of a fixed price, when in fact the contract contained no such guarantee. This error led the people's representatives and citizens to evaluate the decision on inaccurate grounds. The MC emphasizes that the federal authority should not have proceeded from a presumption lacking contractual basis.
### Who read the contract?
An even more disturbing aspect emerges from the report: 'only a few of the people involved read the entire contract'. This means that the result of the negotiations was subjected to insufficient verification before being publicly communicated. It is incomprehensible how the DDPS and Amherd continued to defend the fixed price before Parliament when the document itself did not support it.
The organization of the negotiations itself presented critical gaps. The DDPS entrusted the legal study to an external law firm, Homburger, assigning it alongside the armasuisse arms office. This choice meant that armasuisse's internal legal service remained 'de facto' excluded from contract negotiations. This contradicts the legal mandate of the office, which by definition is the Confederation's specialized procurement center in the field of armaments.
### The delay in communicating to the federal government
A critical element concerns the timing of information to the Federal Council. The first signs of possible additional costs had been received by armasuisse as early as August 2024, and Amherd had been informed of these signals. However, she informed her government colleagues only in March 2025, a delay of approximately seven to eight months. At that point, the United States had confirmed in writing the existence of additional costs.
Even more significant is the timing chosen for the disclosure: two months after the announcement of her resignation and shortly before her departure from the federal government. This timing prevented timely discussion within the government on the issue and raised questions about the transparency of crisis management. The MC considers this behavior 'inadequate'. ### Transparency in Federal Decision-Making and Parliamentary Oversight
The CdG report highlights an essential issue for Switzerland's democratic functioning: Parliament's role in overseeing the executive and the quality of information provided to the people's representatives. When the Federal Council or a department communicate with 'absolute certainty' about facts lacking contractual support, a breach is created between what is claimed and the underlying reality. This practice is particularly serious in cases involving significant public spending.
In the F-35A file, the DDPS repeatedly stated publicly that the price was 'fixed', constructing a political argument based on a false premise. Parliament thus made a decision based on imprecise information, betraying the transparency principle that characterizes Swiss direct democracy. A citizen's right to truthful information is a foundation of popular sovereignty.
### Procedural Problems in Federal Negotiations
The management of F-35A negotiations reveals broader procedural defects in the Confederation's decision-making system. The exclusion of armasuisse's internal legal service in favor of an external firm created fragmentation in the legal verification process. In a specialized procurement center, the internal legal team represents the guardian of contractual and regulatory compliance. Reliance on an external consultant, however competent, does not guarantee the same level of accountability and continuity.
The delay of seven to eight months in communicating the first indications of additional costs to the Federal Council had concrete consequences: - The government was unable to promptly assess the implications for the federal budget - It was not possible to discuss the issue with Parliament before public communications - Negotiations with the United States did not benefit from clear instructions from the government in a timely manner
Amherd, as defense minister, had the obligation to inform the government and the department immediately after being warned in August 2024. The delay until March 2025 represents a serious anomaly in the internal information flow.
### The Impact on Federal Public Spending
The acquisition of F-35A fighter jets is one of the Confederation's most costly defense projects. Decisions in this regard must rest on solid factual grounds and be communicated with precision to the people's representatives. Erring in the communication of the price — presenting it as 'fixed' when it was actually subject to variability — has direct implications for the federal budget and the allocation of public resources.
Parliament, in federal budget proceedings (managed by the Federal Council and approved by the chambers), must have access to correct information to allocate resources according to the Confederation's priorities. Imprecise communication about spending deviates the decision-making process and reduces the effectiveness of parliamentary oversight. The CdG report highlights how even in Switzerland, where controls are generally rigorous, significant procedural gaps can occur when internal oversight bodies do not function adequately.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### The meaning of the report for the future of federal negotiations
The CAG report represents a formal investigation into federal procedures and a concrete opportunity to correct decision-making processes. The Federal Council will have to respond to the Commission's criticism and adopt corrective measures to prevent similar situations from recurring in future important negotiations.
The role of the Commission for Administration — present in both the Chamber of Deputies (National Council) and the Senate (Council of States) — is precisely to oversee the executive, verify that the information provided to Parliament is complete and correct, and supervise public spending management. In the case of F-35A, the Commission identified critical gaps in communication, legal verification, and information timelines. This report sets a precedent for future investigations into federal negotiations of similar magnitude.
### Access to documents and right to administrative information
Swiss citizens have the right to consult federal documents relating to decisions made by the Federal Council and departments. In the case of F-35A negotiations, anyone interested can request copies of documents from the DDPS or the Federal Council following the federal administrative procedures established for access to information.
A concrete first step is to verify whether the full CAG report is available on the official website of the Swiss Parliament (parlament.ch). The report contains detailed findings that provide a factual basis for understanding what went wrong in the negotiations and how the Federal Council communicated with Parliament. This right of access is essential for maintaining transparency and trust in federal institutions.
### The lessons for the federal budget and future procedures
Parliament (National Council and Council of States) approves the federal budget annually and decides to allocate funds for major projects such as the acquisition of F-35A. Before such massive spending decisions, Parliament must receive correct and complete information from the Federal Council. The CAG report serves as a lesson on the need for more rigorous procedures.
The principles that should guide future federal negotiations, according to the Commission's findings, are: - Accurately document every phase of the negotiation from the start - Fully involve internal legal teams of the competent office - Communicate risks and changes to the federal government without delays - Verify and validate every contractual assumption before public communications - Ensure that all people involved have full access to documents
If you wish to deepen your understanding of how decisions and federal spending affect Swiss national taxation and your contribution to the public budget, you will find useful tools to understand the tax system and how your federal taxes fund the services and projects of the Confederation.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/svizzera/politica/1948825/washington-f-35a-berna-concordato-prezzo)*

item.title: Black Day for Novartis: 10% Collapse
item.description: Novartis shares plummet by more than 10% in a day. Lost capitalisation: CHF 24 billion. Two failures in clinical research shake the Swiss pharmaceutical giant.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Tuesday: Novartis collapses by over 10% on the stock exchange - Lost 24 billion CHF in market capitalization in a single day - Cause: two major failures in clinical research
## Key facts
- **What**: Historic collapse of Novartis stock due to two failures in clinical trials - When: Tuesday, from a peak on September 3 (132.68 CHF) to a low (112.06 CHF) - Where: Swiss stock exchange (Basel-based company) - Who: Novartis, Swiss pharmaceutical giant - Amount: Market capitalization reduced from 239 to 215 billion CHF (-24 billion)
Tuesday was a dark day for Novartis. The Basel-based pharmaceutical giant saw its shares plummet by over 10% in the morning, touching a low of 112.06 francs with a loss of almost 13 francs per share. A hemorrhage that, in terms of market value, translates to approximately 24 billion francs evaporated in a single day, bringing capitalization down from 239 to approximately 215 billion francs.
The fall is even more staggering when you consider that just a week earlier, on September 3, the stock had reached an all-time high of 132.68 francs. In one week, Novartis lost over 13% of its market value — a performance that directly impacts the portfolios of thousands of Swiss investors who hold the stock, either directly or through mutual funds or pension instruments.
According to data compiled by the AWP agency, Tuesday's collapse is destined to go down in the annals as the worst daily collapse ever recorded for Novartis, far surpassing previous negative records. It is an event that marks a line in the history of the Swiss stock market, with dimensions even greater than previous financial shocks.
### What triggered the collapse?
The market's reaction reflects disappointment over the recent failures in the development of new drugs. Specifically, on Tuesday, negative results regarding Pelacarsen, a preparation in development against serious cardiovascular risks, were disclosed. At the same time, it emerged that Del-desiran, a product intended for the treatment of a rare muscular disease, had not achieved the desired outcomes in a Phase III study.
Two setbacks within days represented a double blow for investors. For a company that had just touched all-time highs just a week earlier, the consecutive announcement of two failures in clinical research quickly wiped away positive sentiment, transforming it into a rush for the exits. A combination that investors punished severely. An unprecedented collapse. Tuesday's crash represents not only the worst day in Novartis' history, but one of the most significant events in the Swiss stock market in recent years. To understand the severity of what happened, it is enough to compare it with other financial crises that have shaken global markets.
### Comparison with previous crises
In January 2015, when the Swiss National Bank (SNB) decided to end the minimum euro/franc exchange rate, the Swiss market had suffered a loss of 17 billion francs. In March 2020, the arrival of Covid had an impact of 16 billion francs. Even the financial crisis of October 2008 had caused a decline of just over 10 billion francs.
With its 24 billion francs lost in a single day, Novartis has surpassed all these precedents. This is an extreme volatility that directly affects anyone who has investments linked to the shares of the Basel pharmaceutical giant, whether through mutual funds, direct stock portfolios, or finally through the third pillar (3a/3b) or occupational pension (LPP).
### Impact on Swiss investors and savers
For Swiss savers who have invested in the third pillar or pension funds that include Novartis shares, Tuesday's day represents a significant loss of assets. Novartis, together with Roche and other major industrials, is an important component of the SMI (Swiss Market Index), the main index of the Swiss stock exchange. Such a massive collapse has direct effects on the overall performance of the portfolio of anyone who has investments in Swiss equities.
The extreme volatility observed on Tuesday – a loss of Novartis' entire market capitalization that far exceeds that of previous global shocks – highlights the concentrated risks in the Swiss pharmaceutical sector. Two failures in clinical research, announced in rapid succession, were sufficient to demolish tens of billions of value creation accumulated in the months before. To protect wealth, it is advisable to consult [advice on LPP and savings protection](nav:pension) at your bank or a specialized fund manager.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). After such a volatile event, what should a Swiss saver do?
### Analyze your portfolio and rebalance
The first action is to take stock of your exposure to Novartis. If you hold the stock directly, or if you invest in mutual funds that include a significant share of Novartis shares, now is the time for a thorough check. Concentration of risk in a single stock – no matter how important – can expose you to significant losses, as seen on Tuesday.
A classic approach involves rebalancing your portfolio according to your original asset allocation strategy. If before the Novartis crisis, for example, it represented 10% of your portfolio, the 10%+ drop means that its relative weight has decreased (for example to 9%). Rebalancing means realigning the proportion according to the initial plan.
### Consult a financial advisor
Savers with complex or significant portfolios should consult a financial advisor or their bank to evaluate: - Overall exposure to the pharmaceutical sector - Geographic diversification and by asset class - Tax implications of any sales (stamp duties, direct federal tax on capital gains) - Strategies to protect value in the long term
### Available tools
For those investing in the third pillar or occupational pensions, it is possible to contact the fund manager to understand how the fall of Novartis affects the net value of your investment and whether automatic rebalancing options are available. Furthermore, using specialized portfolio tools and consulting experts can help you plan an investment strategy more resilient to future market shocks.
### Don't panic
It is important to remember that a crash of a single stock, no matter how serious, does not necessarily represent a general sell signal for the market. Novartis remains a company with a long history of pharmaceutical innovation. Two failures in the development phase do not erase the intrinsic value of the company in the long term. However, Tuesday's session is a reminder that diversification and regular portfolio monitoring are essential to protect your wealth. Use our [third pillar planning tool](nav:pillar3) to check your investments and adjust them to your risk profile.

item.title: Swiss air traffic grows, but emissions rise
item.description: In 2025, civil aviation surpassed pre-Covid numbers: 1.4 million movements (+5%), 60.5 million passengers (+4%). However, CO2 emissions go up by 3%.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In 2025 Swiss air traffic exceeded pre-Covid figures for the first time - 1.4 million air movements (+5% vs 2024, +3% vs 2019) - 60.5 million passengers (+4% vs 2024), Zurich leading with 32.5 million - CO2 emissions up 3% to 5.74 million tonnes
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss civil aviation exceeds pre-Covid figures in 2025 - When: Data released in 2025 relating to 2025 - Where: Switzerland (main hubs: Zurich, Basel-Mulhouse, Geneva) - Who: FSO (Federal Statistical Office), civil aviation sector - Movements: 1.4 million take-offs and landings, +5% compared to 2024 - Passengers: 60.5 million, +4% vs 2024 - CO2 emissions: 5.74 million tonnes, +3% - Fuel: 1.83 million tonnes supplied in Switzerland
In 2025 Switzerland achieved a significant milestone: civil aviation exceeded for the first time the figures recorded before the Covid-19 crisis. According to data released today by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), air traffic in our country reached 1.4 million movements (take-offs and landings), growing 5% compared to 2024 and 3% compared to 2019, the last year of pre-pandemic normality. A return to pre-Covid levels that marks a consolidation of the recovery in the Swiss aviation sector after years of crisis.
Passenger numbers tell a similar story: the 60.5 million passengers recorded in 2025 represent growth of 4% compared to the previous year and 2% compared to 2019. An expansion that confirms how Swiss air routes have recovered not only pre-pandemic volumes, but have continued to grow beyond that.
### Traffic composition and operational mix
The traffic structure shows interesting operational dynamics. General aviation — which operates predominantly with small-sized aircraft — accounted for approximately 68% of total air movements in Switzerland. Scheduled and charter traffic, on the other hand, dominated the passenger flow with a share of 99% of passengers. This means that the numerical volume of take-offs and landings is largely driven by small aircraft for private and charter use, while the vast majority of passengers — 99 out of 100 — travel on commercial scheduled aircraft.
### Airport hubs: differentiated performance
Switzerland's main airports showed differentiated trends in passenger numbers. Zurich, the largest national and European hub for connecting traffic, recorded a 4% increase reaching 32.5 million annual passengers. Basel-Mulhouse performed even better with an 8% jump, reaching 9.6 million passengers. Geneva, Switzerland's third airport by passenger traffic, remained substantially stable at 17.7 million passengers.
### Flight occupancy and routes
A figure that deserves attention concerns the average occupancy rate of seats on board: it fell from 82% to 79%. Although total passengers grew, airlines increased the supply of seats and flights at a faster pace, compressing the occupancy rate. The overall distance traveled by passengers grew by more than 6%, although the most significant decline in terms of passengers was recorded on routes to North America and Asia, two key regions for Swiss business travel and tourism. ### The Climate Question
With the resumption of air traffic, fuel consumption experienced an inverted contraction. In 2025, approximately 1.83 million tonnes of aircraft fuel were supplied in Switzerland, an increase compared to 1.77 million the previous year. Although the increase is modest in percentage terms, CO2 emissions from these consumptions rose by almost 3%, reaching 5.74 million tonnes of carbon dioxide. Not only that: emissions of nitrogen oxides, an air pollutant that contributes to smog formation and air acidification, grew proportionally to the volume of airport activity.
This dynamic poses an interesting tension in the landscape of Swiss environmental policy. On one hand, the economic and transport recovery is a positive signal. On the other hand, the country's climate commitments require a reduction of overall emissions, regardless of the sector.
### National Implications for Federal Climate Targets
For Switzerland, a country committed to ambitious climate targets—including federal CO2 legislation and reduction targets for 2030 and 2050—the rebound in aviation poses a concrete challenge. Aviation is a 'difficult' sector for decarbonization: unlike road transport, where electric vehicles are spreading rapidly, the absence of mature technological alternatives to fossil fuels for commercial aviation makes emission control more complex.
The 3% growth in aviation CO2 emissions in 2025 coexists with an important historical observation: 2019 recorded even higher levels of emissions and traffic volume. Therefore, from a 20-30 year perspective, the sector will still need to significantly reduce its consumption standards to align with Swiss climate targets.
### European Context and International Pressures
Although UST data does not provide direct benchmarks with other European countries, the growth of Swiss air traffic (+5% annual, +3% cumulative vs 2019) reflects a global dynamic: commercial aviation is recovering quickly from the pandemic and is exceeding pre-Covid levels, while at the same time regulatory and reputational pressure to reduce emissions remains high at federal, cantonal, and international levels. Switzerland has historically maintained environmental standards among the most stringent in Europe, and this data poses an interesting tension between the sector's economic recovery and the Confederation's climate commitments.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### The positive finding: aircraft safety in dramatic improvement
In stark contrast to the negative trend in emissions, Swiss aviation recorded dramatic improvements in aircraft safety in 2025. The number of incidents and serious events involving aircraft registered in Switzerland fell from 23 to 10, representing a reduction of over 50%. This is a particularly significant finding because it was achieved despite airport activity volume increasing substantially.
Accident victims recorded an equally significant decline: from 5 deaths in 2024 to 3 in 2025. Serious injuries, finally, were reduced from 7 to 5. Although every accident and every victim remain tragic from a human perspective, the downward trend — in a context of growing traffic — is a positive indicator of the quality of regulation, maintenance, and operational standards in the Swiss sector.
### What do these figures mean for passengers
For those who fly in Switzerland or with Swiss airlines, the improvement in safety represents a concrete reduction in the statistical risk of serious incidents. Switzerland has historically maintained standards of civil aviation among the most rigorous in the world. The 2025 UST data suggests that this commitment continues to produce tangible results in terms of safety, even during phases of operational expansion. Air traffic control systems, aircraft maintenance protocols, and pilot training remain among the most stringent internationally.
### How and where to learn more
Those wishing to better understand the economic and environmental impact of air traffic on their daily life in Switzerland — both as a passenger and as a taxpayer — can consult the detailed data from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) and monitor how the federal government and cantons integrate these statistics into their sustainable mobility policies. Flight costs, ticket prices, and airport fees affect the national cost of living and the competitiveness of Swiss services in international markets.

item.title: Naturalization Lucerne: permits, costs and procedures
item.description: Complete guide to ordinary naturalization in the Canton of Lucerne: 10 years of residence with C permit, integration requirements and German language B1, times 12-24 months, cantonal and municipal taxes.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - La naturalizzazione ordinaria richiede permesso C e 10 anni di residenza in Svizzera secondo la legislazione federale. - I requisiti specifici variano per cantone e comune; il Canton Lucerna definisce i propri criteri d'integrazione e lingua. - La procedura prevede domanda al comune, valutazione da parte di cantone e Confederazione, e votazione popolare. - Tempi e costi differiscono a seconda della legislazione comunale e cantonale.
## Fatti chiave - **Cosa**: Naturalizzazione ordinaria in Svizzera (acquisizione della cittadinanza dopo residenza stabile) - Quando: Dopo 10 anni di residenza con permesso C; procedura variabile per cantone - Dove: Commissione comunale, uffici cantonali, Segreteria di Stato Migrazione (SEM) - Chi: Candidato straniero, comune, cantone, popolo (votazione) - Requisiti federali: Permesso C, integrazione, padronanza lingua locale, assenza condanne - Competenza: Ogni cantone fissa criteri propri entro quadro federale
### La naturalizzazione ordinaria: un percorso federale-cantonale
La naturalizzazione ordinaria rappresenta il percorso standard per acquisire la cittadinanza svizzera dopo un periodo di residenza stabile nel Paese. Secondo la legislazione federale, il candidato deve disporre di un permesso C di domicilio per almeno 10 anni, oltre a soddisfare requisiti aggiuntivi fissati dai singoli cantoni e comuni. Il Canton Lucerna, come tutti i cantoni svizzeri, gode di competenza autonoma nel definire criteri di integrazione, padronanza linguistica e importi delle tasse, entro il quadro federale.
Il percorso verso la naturalizzazione inizia di norma con un permesso B (dimora, rinnovabile), ottenibile dopo un primo soggiorno legale, o direttamente con permesso C in caso di trasferimento a titolo permanente, per esempio in seguito a matrimonio con cittadino svizzero. Il permesso G, riservato ai frontalieri, non consente accesso diretto alla naturalizzazione ordinaria secondo la legislazione federale, sebbene alcuni cantoni possono prevedere regole specifiche per conteggiare i periodi di frontalieranza; quanto ai dettagli esatti, è necessario verificare con le autorità del canton di residenza.
Una volta raggiunto il decennio di residenza con permesso C, il candidato avvia il procedimento presentando domanda al comune di residenza. Il comune avvia un'istruttoria amministrativa e verifica il rispetto dei criteri federali e cantonali: integrazione sociale, assenza di condanne penali, conoscenza della lingua cantonale, pagamento regolare di imposte e contributi sociali. Successivamente trasmette il fascicolo al cantone. Il Canton Lucerna esamina la pratica secondo la propria legge sulla cittadinanza e, se favorevole, la inoltra alla Segreteria di Stato Migrazione (SEM) federale per il controllo finale. Solo dopo l'assenso federale il dossier ritorna al comune, che sottopone la candidatura al voto popolare. L'esito positivo della votazione conclude la procedura: il candidato acquisisce la cittadinanza svizzera e diritti di voto a livello federale, cantonale e comunale.
### I permessi preliminari e il contesto federale
Prima di accedere alla naturalizzazione ordinaria, il candidato deve trovarsi in una condizione di stabilità amministrativa e legale riconosciuta dalla legge federale sugli stranieri. Il permesso L, della durata massima di un anno, è riservato a soggiorni brevi (turisti, stagionali, rappresentanti diplomatici) e non consente accesso alla naturalizzazione. Il permesso B, detto di dimora, è rinnovabile e consente soggiorno medio-lungo, normalmente per ragioni familiari, di lavoro o umanitarie; la sua durata è variabile e dipende dalle decisioni del cantone. Il permesso C rappresenta il culmine di questa progressione: è concesso dopo una presenza continuativa e rappresenta l'unico prerequisito federale riconosciuto per qualunque procedura di naturalizzazione ordinaria.
La Segreteria di Stato Migrazione (SEM) supervisiona l'applicazione della legge federale sulla cittadinanza svizzera a livello nazionale, garantendo che ogni cantone rispetti i criteri minimi di residenza stabiliti dal Consiglio federale. Tuttavia, la competenza materiale in merito ai criteri d'integrazione, lingua, tasse e procedure rimane in capo al cantone. Ciò significa che il Canton Lucerna, pur dovendo rispettare il vincolo federale dei 10 anni di residenza con permesso C, è libero di richiedere test di integrazione più rigorosi, livelli di competenza linguistica più elevati, o tasse proprie non contemplate dalla normativa federale. ### Federalism and cantons: how the requirements vary
The Swiss system of ordinary naturalization reflects the federalist principle: every canton and municipality enjoys considerable decision-making margin. The Confederation only sets the time requirement (10 years of residence with C permit) and some general eligibility parameters (no criminal convictions, payment of AVS/AI social security contributions, no open tax enforcement), but the procedural details, language tests, integration criteria and tax amounts are the responsibility of the canton.
The Canton of Lucerne regulates ordinary naturalization through its own cantonal law on citizenship. This specific law: the number and type of languages to be known (Lucerne is German-speaking, and basic comprehension and conversation are required), the criteria of social integration (relationship with the community, civic engagement, economic autonomy), the times of evaluation by the municipal and cantonal authorities, and the amount of fees to be paid by the candidate. The municipalities of Lucerne also have additional autonomy: some municipalities may have faster procedures, others more rigid; some municipalities provide for preliminary information meetings or periods of informal 'observation' before the formal application.
The overall times vary accordingly. At the federal level, once the canton has approved the application and forwarded it to the SEM, federal control normally takes 2–6 months.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Apply in Your Canton
The first step towards ordinary naturalization is to contact the competent office of your municipality of residence. In the Canton of Lucerne, each municipality has a municipal integration or citizenship official, often integrated into the police office or municipal civil affairs. The citizen must make an appointment and preliminarily verify that they hold a Type C permit and have achieved 10 years of continuous residence in Switzerland. Once these preliminary details are confirmed, the municipality provides an official application form, a detailed checklist of required documents, and instructions on the local linguistic evaluation officers.
Typical documentation includes: certificate of extract from the criminal record registry (to verify absence of criminal convictions), proof of payment of AVS/AI social security contributions over the last 10 years, proof of regular payment of federal, cantonal and municipal taxes for the last 3–5 years, valid LAMal health insurance certificates, a personal letter of motivation for the application, sometimes references from employers or teachers of German language courses. Some Lucerne municipalities also require a certificate of attendance at a German language B1 course or equivalent, from a recognized language school or from public institutions. Once all documents are collected, the candidate submits the completed application and pays the preliminary admission fees (a municipal fee varying between municipalities, generally between CHF 100 and CHF 500).
The municipal office initiates the instructional process (normally 2–4 months), during which it verifies the absence of criminal sanctions, contacts the employer for confirmation of employment, consults the cantonal social services to verify no dependency on subsidies, and organizes linguistic evaluation and integration interviews with qualified personnel. If the local opinion is positive, the file is sent to the canton. The cantonal office (the Citizenship Division or equivalent structure according to current organization) completes the examination of the case (another 3–6 months) and, if it approves, transmits it to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) in Bern. The SEM carries out the final federal control (1–3 months), verifying mainly the absence of reasons of national security that would oppose recognition.
### Popular Vote and Citizenship Acquisition
Once federal approval from the SEM is obtained, the file returns to the municipality, which schedules a popular vote (municipal assembly, paper ballot, or electronic ballot according to municipal customs). Swiss citizens of the municipality vote on the candidacy; the positive vote of the population formalizes the acquisition of Swiss citizenship. The entire path from the first informal consultation to the recognition of citizenship normally takes 12–24 months, although it can be shortened to 9 months in municipalities with efficient procedures or with candidates of excellent integration and administrative situation.
At the end of the procedure and with citizenship acquired, the candidate receives an official document recognizing citizenship and becomes eligible to exercise political rights (right to vote and eligibility) at federal, cantonal and municipal level from the moment of official publication of the decision.
### Verify Details with Your Municipality
Since the Canton of Lucerne and its municipalities have their own competences regarding language tests, integration criteria, fee amounts, voting procedures and timelines, it is essential to contact DIRECTLY your municipality office before applying. Not all general information provided above applies to every Lucerne municipality. The municipal office will provide updated information material, a precise checklist of documents specifically required by your municipality, references to local German language courses subsidized by public bodies, submission deadlines and direct contacts of evaluators. For federal questions (for example on calculation of frontier periods, foreign permits, or reasons for federal rejection), contact the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) via the official portal www.sem.admin.ch; always check direct federal guidelines from the national portal, not from cantonal sites, for regulatory accuracy.
Calculate your timelines and costs using our [tax and administrative cost calculator](nav:calculator) and verify whether your cantonal and municipal taxes have been paid regularly by consulting your [Lucerne cantonal tax return](nav:tax-return). Contact your Lucerne municipality right away to begin your journey towards Swiss citizenship.

item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 1,700 diplomated nurses abandon the sector every year in Switzerland - 75% starts in hospital, but 47% remains at age 40 - VPOD demands reduced working hours at equal pay and salary revaluation
## Key Facts - **What**: Massive shortage of healthcare professionals in Switzerland - Source: Obsan (Swiss Health Observatory), recent report - Key data: 1,700 diplomated nurses abandon the sector every year - Critical percentages: 75% starts in an institution, 47% remains at age 40 - Main actor: VPOD trade union demands immediate action - Temporary solution: Resort to healthcare assistants (OSS), insufficient
The Swiss Health Observatory has sounded yet another alarm: more and more healthcare professionals are abandoning medicine and nursing. This is not a marginal phenomenon. According to the Obsan report, the country is missing approximately 1,700 diplomated nurses per year — a figure that does not even account for those who, after completing their training, nonetheless decide to leave the sector.
The numbers speak for themselves. 75% of people who graduated in nursing care at the tertiary level start working in a healthcare institution. But it is not a stable achievement. At age 40, this percentage drops to about 47%: almost one in two have abandoned the profession. A hemorrhage of expertise that puts at risk the ability of the Swiss healthcare system to provide quality care.
The VPOD trade union denounces the causes: underpaid workers, tasks that do not match the skills acquired, unsustainable stress levels. This is not an abstract criticism — it is the direct reflection of reality in wards and departments. Pressure has increased, staffing levels remain insufficient, wages do not keep pace with inflation. The result is predictable: those who have the skills leave.
### The temporary solution that doesn't work
Currently, the system compensates for the shortage by resorting to healthcare assistants (OSS), who have professional training at secondary level II. It is a patch, not a cure. And the OSS are beginning to flee as well. If diplomated workers, with a higher qualification, are leaving en masse, why should the OSS stay? The answer is obvious: they don't.
VPOD is explicit in calling for a change of course. It is not 'save money and work ever more intensely'. The request is the opposite: invest in the healthcare system, not empty it. The union focuses on improved working conditions with a significant reduction in working hours at equal pay, the revaluation of all healthcare professions — which, being heavily feminized, suffer from inadequate recognition and remuneration — and mandatory support for newly graduated professionals, particularly in the first years of their career. ### What these numbers mean for access to care
Staff shortages are not an administrative abstraction. It has concrete effects on the daily lives of those who live and work in Switzerland. Hospitals and healthcare facilities must manage the same number of patients with fewer qualified staff — resulting in longer waiting lists, higher risks of error, and declining quality of service.
The Swiss health system, however advanced, depends on the availability of qualified personnel. When 53% of tertiary graduates drop out by the age of 40, it is not a matter of natural turnover — it is a net loss of public and private investment in training. Every student who completes their Bachelor's Degree in Nursing has benefited from public resources (scholarships, training, internships). If you give up after 5-10 years of work, the return on thatinvestment is negative.
The initiative on nursing care, approved by an overwhelming majority of the Swiss population, should already address these issues. But the VPOD points out that five years after its approval, concrete progress remains insufficient. This means that the commitments made by the federal and cantonal levels have not yet translated into tangible improvements in wages, hours or working conditions.
### The burden on cantons and structures
This crisis has a federal dimension, but affects it differently at the cantonal level.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What Changes for Healthcare Workers
If you are a qualified or trainee nurse, here is the picture: your profession is in high demand, but working conditions do not automatically improve. VPOD's demands — reduction of working hours at equal salary, revaluation of feminized professions, support for newly graduated professionals — have not yet been implemented on a large scale.
The first step is union dialogue. VPOD represents thousands of workers in the Swiss public and social sector, including healthcare. If you are not a member, considering membership means accessing union support, collective campaigns for improved working conditions, and representation in negotiations. It is not a guarantee of immediate success, but it is the channel through which pressure on hospital management and cantonal governments is realized.
Second, consult current salary data for your canton and your level of qualification. A correct Swiss paycheck must reflect your position and qualifications. If you notice significant discrepancies from the standards, it is not irrational to consider cantonal mobility or further training. Continuing education in healthcare is almost always valued by healthcare facilities.
Third, if you are in training and are considering leaving, speak with a mentor or with your canton's vocational guidance service. Statistics show that 53% leave within 40 years — but this is not destiny. It is the result of unsustainable working conditions, not personal incompetence.
### What to Do If You Are a Healthcare Employer
If you manage a healthcare facility, the message from Obsan and VPOD is clear: competition for talent is even more intense. Recruiting and retaining qualified personnel is not optional — it is central to your facility's survival. Policies for reducing working hours at equal salary, loyalty bonuses, mentorship programs for newly graduated professionals are not abstract additional costs — they are investments in operational stability.
To deepen your understanding of the evolution of the Swiss healthcare labor market and career opportunities, consult specialized job postings in the healthcare sector and monitor job announcements from facilities that are investing in attracting and retaining personnel.

item.title: Pension funds: return boom in 2025
item.description: Swiss pension funds archive 2025 with an average return of 6.3%, driven by equities. Stable conversion rate at 5.20% for future annuities.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Swiss pension funds: yield +6.3% in 2025, all-time high in the last 20 years - Shares reach 34% of the portfolio, bonds at historic lows - In 2026 confirmed trend: +5% until August, stable conversion rate at 5.20%
## Key facts - **What**: Exceptional returns from Swiss pension funds, driven by shares and alternative investments - When: 2025 and 2026 (until August) - Where: Switzerland (469 pension funds, 80% sector equity) - Who: Complement (consulting company), Swiss pension funds - Amount: 6.3% (2025), 5% (2026), CHF 77 billion returns vs CHF 67 billion paid - Historical benchmark: Twenty-year average of 3.6% per year far exceeded
Swiss pension funds closed 2025 with an extraordinary performance: average return of 6.3%, well above the twenty-year average of 3.6% per year. The study published today by the consulting firm Complementa, based on data from 469 pension funds covering around 80% of the sector's total assets, reveals a clear shift towards venture capital. Stocks reached 34% of the portfolio — the highest value ever recorded in the history of the Swiss system. Meanwhile, the bond allocation fell to a new all-time low. The positive trend continues in 2026: until August, yields stand at a further +5%.
### The 'third taxpayer': when financial markets work for the ### How the extraordinary 2025 impacts future pensions
Pension funds have decided to apply an average conversion rate of 5.20% to the capital accumulated at the time of retirement (age 65). [Discover how to calculate your pension](nav:pension). According to Complementa's projections, this value could remain substantially stable over the next five years, providing predictability for those approaching retirement. The conversion rate is crucial: it determines how much monthly pension the retiree will receive from the accumulated capital. A higher average return — such as the 6.3% in 2025 — means larger capital sums at the time of withdrawal from the labor market, and therefore potentially higher pensions once the conversion coefficient is applied.
However, it is important to consider that the conversion rate remains compressed by current extremely low interest rates and the increase in life expectancy. A rate of 5.20% is higher than the lowest historical average of recent years, but remains modest when compared to previous generations. This means that someone who has accumulated 500,000 francs will receive an annual pension of approximately 26,000 francs (500,000 × 5.2%), equal to approximately 2,167 francs monthly. For this reason, the exceptional returns of 2025 and 2026 function as a 'cushion' against inflation erosion of future pensions.
### The hidden risk: illiquid investments and market volatility
While on one hand returns have been extraordinary, on the other hand pension funds are exposing themselves to new risks. The growing allocation towards illiquid investments (real estate, mortgages, alternatives) offers stability in normal economic cycles, but reduces the operational flexibility of the funds. Should a severe real estate crisis occur or tensions in European sovereign debt, the funds could find themselves in the difficult situation of being unable to quickly liquidate positions to meet massive pension withdrawals. Furthermore, a decline in real estate prices would have a direct impact on the book value of assets and potentially on future pensions. This explains why Complementa's specialists warn against the risks of excessive confidence in current markets, emphasizing that 'diversification is not negative, but it carries risks.'
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Check Your Balance and Calculate Your Expected Pension
Every Swiss worker affiliated with a pension fund [LPP/BVG](nav:pension) has the right to receive an annual statement of account reporting the accumulated capital, returns, and pension projections. If you have not received this document, it's time to contact your pension fund directly (the name is on your pay slip). The procedure to calculate your expected pension is simple and follows three steps:
1. Retrieve your latest statement of account from your pension fund (paper or online platform), which can be accessed on the fund's website or requested via email from the administrative office. 2. Verify the accumulated capital as of December 31st of the previous year. This is the gross value on which your future pension is calculated. 3. Apply the conversion rate (5.20% national average, but may vary slightly between funds). Multiply the capital by 5.2% (0.052) to get the estimated annual pension.
Numerical example: If you have accumulated 400,000 francs and your fund applies 5.20%, the annual pension will be approximately 20,800 francs (400,000 × 0.052), equal to 1,733 francs gross monthly. Of course, this is the gross amount; cantonal taxes on pension income will further reduce the net amount in your pocket.
### Where to Find Information Specific to Your Fund
If you want to explore the specific returns of your pension fund (not the national average of 6.3%), access the fund's web platform or contact the administrative office directly. Many funds also provide personalized projections up to age 65, taking into account inflation and market evolution. The Complementa study involved 469 funds out of thousands in Switzerland: yours could have a slightly higher or lower performance than average. To plan your post-retirement budget precisely, ask your fund for a certified projection if you are less than 10 years from retirement.
Next steps: Use the [pension calculator](nav:pension) to simulate different scenarios based on current data from your personal situation.

item.title: Ticino minimum wage at risk: 4,000 workers excluded
item.description: On September 7, 2026, it withdraws the popular initiative, but the Ettlin motion risks nullifying the benefits for 67% of catering workers. At risk 316 francs per month increase.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Ticino minimum wage: 21.75-22.25 CHF/hour by 2029 - Monthly increase: 316 francs for the 23,000 beneficiaries - At risk: 4,000 workers due to Ettlin motion (June 2026) - 67% of 4,000 in hospitality sector
## Key facts - **What**: Introduction of Ticino minimum wage + risk of exclusion from Ettlin motion - When: September 7, 2026 (initiative withdrawal), April 20, 2026 (Parliament approval), June 2026 (federal motion) - Where: Ticino, hospitality and hotel sector - Who: Socialist Party, Federal Parliament, Federal Chambers - Amount: 21.75-22.25 CHF/hour by 2029, increase of 316 CHF monthly - Beneficiaries at risk: 4,000 out of 23,000 workers
Fabrizio Sirica, co-president of the Socialist Party, officially withdrew the popular initiative for 'Social Minimum Wage' on Monday, September 7, 2026. The withdrawal followed the political agreement between parties and the absence of appeals against the legislative amendments approved by Parliament on April 20, 2026. With no referendum currently underway against this regulation, the new Ticino minimum wage will soon come into force without going to a popular vote.
### The new minimum wage in Ticino
The new legislation will bring the Ticino minimum wage to a range between 21.75 and 22.25 francs per hour by 2029, an increase of 1.75 francs from the current level. This change will have a direct impact on approximately 23,000 low-income workers in the canton. Each beneficiary would see their monthly salary increase by at least 316 francs, a tangible figure that improves the ability to cope with the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Ticino. The Socialist Party expressed great satisfaction with the result achieved in the political compromise.
But a federal obstacle threatens to nullify these benefits. In June 2026, the federal chambers adopted the bill resulting from the so-called 'Ettlin motion', which gives priority to wages set in collective agreements declared to have general binding force over those established by the Cantons. If this regulation were to come into force, approximately 4,000 of the 23,000 Ticino beneficiaries would risk being excluded from the benefit. ### Who risks losing the raise
The category mainly affected by the Ettlin motion is that of restaurants and hotels. 67% of the 4,000 workers at risk reside in Ticino and operate in these sectors. For these professionals, the practical effect would be the non-use of the benefits of the new cantonal rule, if their collective bargaining agreement already applied federally fixed wages with precedence over the cantonal provisions.
The situation creates involuntary discrimination between workers in the same canton. A cook or waitress in the Ticino catering sector may not receive the increase of CHF 1.75/hour, while a colleague in another sector does, depending exclusively on the applicability of the federal collective agreement in his branch of activity.
### The conflict between federalism and cantonal politics
The Socialist Party has highlighted that this situation represents a potential violation of cantonal competences in the field of social policy. According to the SP, a federal decision limiting or nullifying the effect of a cantonal rule constitutes an attack on the principle of Swiss federalism. The cantons have historically had the power to define their own wage and social policies, and a federal imposition that restricts their application raises relevant questions of the proper distribution of powers between levels of government.
### Concrete economic consequences
For the catering sector
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Verify Your Collective Agreement
For interested Ticino workers, the first step is to verify your collective labor agreement. If you work in the restaurant or hospitality sector, carefully check whether your contract contains minimum salary clauses set at the federal level and declared to be of general applicability. If so, your salary may be subject to the federal priority provided by the Ettlin motion, regardless of the new Ticino cantonal regulation. Familiarize yourself with how to correctly read your [payslip](nav:payslip), so you can immediately recognize the effect of the increase once implemented.
The second step is to monitor the outcome of the ongoing referendums. If the Socialist Party manages to collect the necessary signatures and bring the Ettlin motion to popular vote, the result could determine the fate of the federal regulation. A rejection by Swiss voters would prevent the motion from coming into force, ensuring the 23'000 Ticino beneficiaries full access to the new minimum salary of 21.75-22.25 CHF/hour without sectoral limitations.
### Possible Scenarios by 2029
If the Ettlin motion were to come into force without modifications, the Ticino minimum salary would only apply to workers whose collective agreement does NOT provide salaries set and declared as mandatory at the federal level. This would create a two-tier situation: some workers in the restaurant sector would receive the increase of up to 316 francs per month, others would not, depending on the applicability of their specific contract. For those excluded, the status quo would continue until the federal contract were renegotiated.
Conversely, if the referendum were to block the Ettlin motion before it came into force, the Ticino minimum salary would apply uniformly to all 23'000 beneficiaries by 2029, regardless of federal collective agreements. In this scenario, the political agreement reached on April 20, 2026 by Parliament would have full effect without exceptions.
### Calculate Your New Salary
To have an accurate estimate of what your new monthly salary would be with the increase of 1.75 CHF/hour, you can use [Frontaliere Ticino's salary calculator](nav:calculator). By entering your current hourly salary and the number of hours worked weekly, you will be able to simulate the effect of the increase once the Ticino regulation comes fully into force. This tool allows you to plan your personal budget and concretely assess the impact of the federal decision on your income situation.

item.title: Novartis Plummets 10% in Stock Exchange for Failed Studies
item.description: Pelacarsen and Del-desiran fail clinical trials. Capitalization down CHF 24 billion, the most severe collapse in history.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Novartis plummets over 10%, loses CHF 24 billion in market capitalization - Two failed studies on cardiovascular and neuromuscular treatments - It's the worst stock collapse ever recorded in its history
## Key facts - **What**: Stock market collapse of 10% - Amount: CHF 24 billion lost, price down to 112.06 CHF (–13 CHF per share) - Causes: Failure of Pelacarsen (cardiovascular) and Del-desiran (rare muscular disease) studies - Market capitalization: Fell from CHF 239 to CHF 215 billion - Record: Worst daily collapse ever recorded for Novartis - Historical comparison: Exceeds SNB losses in 2015 (–17 bn), Covid 2020 (–16 bn), 2008 (–10+ bn)
Novartis shares experienced one of the worst days in their history. The share of the Basel-based pharmaceutical giant collapsed by more than 10% in the morning, touching a low of 112.06 francs, with a loss of nearly 13 francs per share. A massive evaporation of value that translates to approximately 24 billion francs: market capitalization fell from 239 to approximately 215 billion francs.
The fall is all the more dizzying when compared to the recent past. Just a week ago, on September 3rd, the share had touched a historic high of 132.68 francs. The drop from peak to low wiped out every gain of the week in just a few hours.
### The worst collapse in Novartis's history
According to data processed by the Awp agency, the crash is destined to go down in the annals as the worst daily collapse ever recorded. To give historical perspective on the severity: the end of the euro/franc minimum exchange rate decreed by the SNB in January 2015 had wiped out 'only' 17 billion francs, the arrival of Covid in March 2020 had an impact of 16 billion, while the financial crisis of October 2008 had caused a drop of just over 10 billion. Novartis has far surpassed all these precedents in a single trading session.
Market reaction reflects disappointment over recent failures in clinical research. Yesterday, negative results were disclosed regarding Pelacarsen, a treatment in development against serious cardiovascular risks. Today it emerged that Del-desiran, a product intended for the treatment of a rare muscular disease, did not achieve the expected outcomes in a phase III study. Two clinical setbacks announced in just a few days triggered panic among investors, triggering cascading sell orders. ### Direct impact on Swiss pension funds and investors
Novartis is not a marginal stock in the Swiss portfolio. As one of the world's three largest pharmaceutical manufacturers, headquartered in Basel and listed on the Swiss stock exchange, Novartis is a historic and massive component of the SMI and SPI indices. It is ubiquitous in supplementary pension funds (LPP/BVG) of those who work in Switzerland and frequent in third pillar investments (3a) of those who want to diversify their savings.
A collapse of this magnitude generates direct and tangible losses. Corporate pension funds that include the security see the value of assets decline: a loss of 24 billion from the security is proportionally reflected in savers' accounts. Those who have invested in the 3a through Swiss equity funds suffer an immediate contraction in net worth. Investors who own Novartis shares directly cash out less in a potential sale these days than they did a week ago.
Although a single session crash is dramatic in the short term, the history of Swiss markets offers a more reassuring prospect. After the abolition of the minimum euro/franc exchange rate (January 2015) and the Covid collapse (March 2020), Swiss indices recovered in the medium to long term, albeit with volatility. However, the immediate psychological damage is real: trust in Swiss pharmaceutical stocks takes a significant hit.
### Because Novartis is different from
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to check if you are exposed to the Novartis collapse
If you are a Swiss investor or saver, this collapse potentially affects you. Here is the procedure to understand your exposure:
Step 1: Check your bank account or broker. If you own Novartis shares directly, you will see the decline reflected instantly in your account statement. Access your bank's or broker's online portal, search for Novartis in your portfolio, note the number of shares and the current price. By multiplying these two numbers you will have the current value of your position.
Step 2: Check your LPP/BVG pension funds. Request from your employer or directly from the pension fund the documents showing the composition of the insurance portfolio. If the fund includes Swiss equities (often referred to as SMI tracker or SPI tracker), Novartis is almost certainly included. The 10% reduction in the share translates into a proportional contraction in the value of your pension position: if the fund is composed of 2% Novartis, the collapse costs you approximately 0.2% of the total value.
Step 3: Check your third pillar 3a. If you have opened a 3a account at a bank and have chosen active management or an equity fund, it may contain Novartis. Request the statement of portfolio composition. This information is crucial because the 3a often represents your main tool for tax savings and pension protection: knowing what it contains is essential.
### What to do in the coming days
Don't give in to panic. A black day does not mean the end of Novartis. The company remains one of the three pharmaceutical giants in the world with a broad portfolio of medicines already on the market that generate billions in annual revenue. The failures of Pelacarsen and Del-desiran are serious from the perspective of future research, but they do not eliminate the drugs that Novartis sells today in global markets.
Assess your overall risk profile. If today's Novartis collapse has caused you anxiety or insomnia, it is a signal: perhaps your total portfolio is too exposed to equities compared to your true risk tolerance. A professional review of the allocation between stocks and bonds (asset allocation) may be appropriate: an independent financial specialist can help you recalibrate based on your age, time horizon and concrete objectives.
Following developments is essential. Novartis could recover significantly in the coming months if other products in development show positive results in clinical trials. Conversely, if other trials fail, the stock could suffer further. Stay informed through [official Novartis financial reports and consult your pension management tools](nav:pension) to maintain conscious control of your investment choices.

item.title: Nurses: shortage by 2034 in Switzerland
item.description: The 4th Obsan report predicts a severe shortage of nurses by 2034. Only 55% of the needs are covered by personnel trained in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - By 2034 aggravated shortage of nurses in Switzerland - Maximum coverage rate: 55% with trained Swiss staff - Early release: 75% graduates remain immediately, only 47% at 40 years of age - Two factors: 1/3 staff replacement + population ageing
## Key facts - **What**: Nursing staff shortage by 2034 - When: Screening period 2024–2034 - Who: Swiss Health Observatory (Obsan) - Where: Swiss health institutions at national level - Coverage rate: 40%–55% for tertiary education in Switzerland - Early release: 75% after graduation, 47% at age 40 - Report: 4th Obsan report published recently
Switzerland is preparing for an unprecedented health challenge. According to the 4th report of the Swiss Health Observatory (Obsan), the country will face an aggravated shortage of health personnel by 2034, with particular pressure on the nursing sector. The most critical data is immediate: the coverage rate of staff needs by those trained in Switzerland will not exceed 55% for nurses.
At the level of nursing care (tertiary), the projections indicate that the share of needs covered by training in the Confederation will be between 40% and 55% in the period 2024–2034. This time window is already upon us and the situation is getting worse every year.
### Two critical factors behind the crisis
Obsan's report identifies two drivers ### The alarm from unions: working conditions are the critical issue
Reactions to the Obsan report came quickly. The Swiss Association of Nurses (ASI) highlighted an unequivocal message: 'We must succeed in keeping qualified healthcare workers in the profession. For this, better working conditions are needed everywhere'. The Association sees in the Nursing Care Initiative, particularly in its second phase, 'a golden opportunity for political leaders to effectively combat the shortage and improve the framework conditions in a targeted way'.
The Swiss Public Services Union (VPOD/SSP) raised an even stronger alarm, describing the situation as 'concerning'. The VPOD does not ask for generic solutions, but concrete public investments to ensure sufficient staff, acceptable working conditions, and quality healthcare accessible to everyone. The message is clear: without addressing the problem of working conditions, no training program will be enough.
### Why nurses leave so soon
The figures on early exits hint at the real underlying problem. Although the Obsan report does not analyze in detail the personal reasons, the statements from ASI and VPOD clearly suggest the factors: excessive workload, heavy shifts, salaries insufficient compared to responsibility and physical and psychological strain, and lack of professional recognition. The decline from 75% to 47% between the first year of work and 40 years of age indicates that 40% of nurses trained in Switzerland decide to completely change direction in their career.
This is not a 'natural exodus' towards retirement. It is the premature departure of professionals in the prime of their competence. It means losing accumulated experience, forcing colleagues to fill the gap, and creating a vicious circle where working conditions deteriorate further. Hence the imperative need, according to unions, to prioritize addressing working conditions rather than focusing only on training new nurses.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What must change: the role of federal institutions, cantons and hospitals
The Obsan report provides the diagnosis; now concrete solutions are needed. At the federal level, the Federal Council and Parliament must recognize that the shortage of nurses by 2034 is not purely a demographic issue, but a crisis of sustainability in the national health system. This requires structural public investment, not just declarations of intent. Cantons play an even more central role: many directly manage hospitals and healthcare facilities and oversee professional training competencies at the tertiary level.
Improving nurses' salaries, reducing the number and intensity of shifts, investing in safer and more dignified work environments: these decisions fall to the cantons and healthcare institutions. The Nursing Care Initiative, of which the second phase represents the legislative tool to advance reforms, must become concrete and not remain on paper. Each canton must adapt measures to its own context, but the commitment must be federal.
### Training and strategic international recruitment
Regarding the supply of healthcare professionals trained in Switzerland, nursing schools must be adequately funded. The fact that the coverage rate remains between 40% and 55% for the 2024–2034 period means that Switzerland will necessarily have to rely on international recruitment to fill the structural gap. This poses new challenges: integration of foreign professionals, formal recognition of foreign diplomas, management of language and working culture in Swiss facilities, and regulatory compliance with international agreements.
### What to do concretely going forward
For those working in the healthcare sector or considering a nursing career, the moment is critical and, paradoxically, favorable. The predicted shortage entails both risks and opportunities: on one hand, greater workload and potential stress; on the other, greater demand for professionals and wider margin to negotiate better working conditions. [Discover job opportunities in the Swiss healthcare sector](nav:jobs) and evaluate your positioning in the market. If you are already an employed professional in Switzerland, [check your payslip and your Swiss tax and pension obligations](nav:payslip): understanding your compensation package is essential to negotiate improvements. Finally, remember that the Swiss healthcare system is based on [mandatory LAMal/KVG coverage for all residents](nav:health): any change in the availability of nursing staff can directly impact the quality and accessibility of the care you receive and your health protection.

item.title: Migros online: +21,000 products in Regensdorf
item.description: New logistics hub in Regensdorf (ZH) with 60% more products, 7,500 orders/day, 200-500 jobs. Same-day deliveries to Zurich by February 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Migros doubles online assortment: 12,500 → 21,000 products (+60%) - Hub Regensdorf handles 7,500 orders/day on 38,000 m² over 4 floors - Target 70% capacity by February 2027; 200-500 employees - Revenue CHF 362 million, 47% Swiss online market
## Key facts - **What**: New Migros Online logistics centre in Regensdorf, Zurich - When: May 2026 (phased), 70% capacity by February 2027 - Where: Regensdorf (ZH); replaces Pratteln (BL) and Bremgarten (AG) - Who: Migros, manager Katrin Tschannen - Capacity: 7,500 orders/day, 200-500 employees - Turnover: CHF 362 million (2025), market share 47% - Growth: +17% orders August vs previous year, +12% turnover
Migros accelerates online commerce with the new Regensdorf distribution center. Gradually put into operation at the end of May, the logistics hub represents the decisive step in the digital strategy of the main Swiss chain in a very competitive market: Migros Online has 47% of the national e-commerce market share, while Coop.ch holds 48%.
The assortment available on the online platform increases by 60%, from 12,500 to 21,000 products. The offer thus reaches the breadth of a traditional MMM supermarket, bridging the gap between digital catalogue and physical store. The new hub, built on approximately 38,000 square metres spread over four floors, has an operating capacity of 7,500 orders per day.
### Phase ## Economic and Employment Implications
The ramp-up of the Regensdorf center reflects a precise strategy by Migros to capitalize on e-commerce growth in Switzerland. The past two years have shown that previous logistics capacity was insufficient. In August alone, online orders increased by 17% compared to the same period of the previous year, and the division's revenue grew by 12%. Migros Online achieved annual revenue of 362 million francs last year, positioning itself in a close battle with Coop.ch for digital market leadership: 47% market share against 48% for its main competitor.
According to Katrin Tschannen, head of the division, the bet on growth is firm: the stated goal is average annual growth exceeding 10%. This means that the new center was not oversized for the present, but designed as flexible infrastructure that will support expansion in the coming years.
### Delivery Speed and Competitive Advantages
Greater logistics capacity enables significant reductions in delivery times. In the Zurich metropolitan area, within the medium term, same-day deliveries will be possible. This represents a competitive advantage in a highly densified region where orders are concentrated. Fulfillment speed is increasingly a decisive factor in consumers' choice between digital platforms, especially for fresh products.
### Managing Initial Shortfalls
The gradual launch of the facility had caused temporary gaps in the online shop, particularly for some fresh products. Migros is currently working to resolve these continuity issues. Full achievement of operational capacity by February 2027 should stabilize the offering across all product categories.
### Impact on the Swiss Labor Market
From an employment perspective, the new center represents an investment in the logistics infrastructure of German-speaking Switzerland. The relocation of 250 employees from Pratteln and Bremgarten to Regensdorf, with three-quarters of them accepting, demonstrates the company's willingness to maintain employment continuity despite logistics consolidation. The expansion to 200-500 positions in the new hub generates positive dynamics for the Zurich area, historically a hub of attraction for the Swiss supply chain and the tertiary sector labor market.

On the consumer front, Migros Online's expansion to 21,000 products (from the previous base of 12,500) means significantly increased choice. For those living or working in German-speaking Switzerland, particularly around Zurich and in the Regensdorf area, the service will become progressively more convenient and faster.

The further development planned in French-speaking Switzerland (a 60,000 m² project with 400-500 employees for the basin served by Ecublens) suggests that Migros will continue to invest in territorial logistics capacity.
